title: Oregon will not prosecute baby's abuser because the child is too young to testify
text: An Oregon couple posted on social media this week seeking justice for their one-year-old son, Jacob, who was beaten by a babysitter two months ago. Photographs posted to Facebook show scrapes, cuts, a black eye and deep bruises on the baby's face and arms that resulted from the assault. “The first thing I saw was a black eye. I thought maybe marker got on his face or something. When he turned over, his whole right side of his face black and blue.” Quinney said. Quinney told Oregon Live that she knew immediately that the babysitter had injured him. She took Jacob to the hospital, where police met her and opened an investigation into the assault. Prosecutors later informed Jacob's parents that no charges will be filed against the person responsible for the injuries. According to Oregon Live, Washington County Deputy District Attorney Dustin Staten emailed Quinney a link to a story published by The Oregonian/OregonLive describing the difficulties the law creates for prosecutors. The story's headline read: “Even pets are better protected than young kids under Oregon abuse laws, prosecutors say.” The article explained that, to convict a suspected child abuser of felony assault or criminal mistreatment, prosecutors must prove under Oregon law that the victim suffered a physical injury, which means proving that the child experienced substantial pain. The article states: “Appellate rulings have made that hard to prove if victims can't talk about the extent of their suffering.”

title: Wall Street showman Scaramucci handed keys to Trump's communications machine!
text: Trump has made his pick, and it is a Wall Street loyalist. President Donald Trump tapped financier Anthony Scaramucci, a long-time supporter, as his White House communications director on Friday, a White House official said. Scaramucci, currently at the Export-Import Bank, is expected to start his new job in August, the official said. And the rest of the team? No other changes were immediately expected in a communications operation that includes press secretary Sean Spicer and his deputy, Sarah Sanders, the official said. The timing could hardly be more dramatic. The appointment lands as the White House battles questions over a special counsel probe and several congressional investigations into alleged Russian meddling in the 2016 U.S. presidential election and possible collusion with Trump's campaign. The communications job has sat empty since Michael Dubke quit as communications director in May. Since then, Spicer has been juggling both roles, press secretary and communications director. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Trump interviewed Scaramucci on Friday morning and the job was offered and accepted. Scaramucci, a Republican fundraiser and founder of Skybridge Capital, had earlier been offered the post of U.S. ambassador to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development in Paris.

title: House blasts through $696 billion defense bill in massive win for Trump's military dreams
text: Trump wanted a bigger, stronger military, and the House just delivered. The U.S. House of Representatives passed its version of a massive annual defense bill on Friday, dodging explosive amendments on transgender troops and climate policy. The vote was a crushing 344-81 to pass the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which sets military policy and authorizes up to a staggering $696 billion in spending for the Department of Defense. And it was not just Republicans. Showing just how bipartisan the appetite for defense dollars is in Congress, 117 Democrats joined 227 Republicans in backing the measure. Only eight Republicans and 73 Democrats voted no. But the fight is far from over. The bill faces more hurdles before it can become law, notably because it would push military spending beyond last year's $619 billion bill, defying “sequestration” caps on government spending set in the 2011 Budget Control Act. Trump wants to pay for the military boost by slashing nondefense spending. His fellow Republicans control both the House and Senate, but they will need Senate Democrats, who want to increase military spending, for Trump's plans to take effect. The House NDAA also pumps up missile defense spending by 25 percent, adds thousands more active-duty troops to the Army, gives the Navy five new ships and hands U.S. troops a 2.4 percent raise, their biggest in eight years. And it creates a brand-new Space Corps military service, pushed by lawmakers alarmed by China and Russia's activities in space, but opposed by Defense Secretary Jim Mattis! The Senate votes on its version later this year, and the two must be reconciled before the measure reaches the White House for Trump to sign into law or veto.

title: Pharmaceutical companies target profits in rare diseases
text: All of the world's most expensive drugs are used to treat uncommon conditions. It might be assumed that pharmaceutical companies earn most of their profit from drugs for well-known diseases, but new research shows that they are instead searching for the next “big thing” in rare diseases. The industry's profit margins continue to rise considerably with rarer diseases, because companies can charge more for these drugs than for medication for more common conditions. The search for the next profitable product among rare diseases has halted some advances in treating more common conditions, which may explain why no cure has been found for some of the most common diseases affecting the world's population. In 1983, the Orphan Drug Act began providing incentives for the development of drugs for rarer diseases, to ensure that people with uncommon conditions were not overlooked in new scientific research because such drugs were less profitable. Because of these incentives, which include reduced taxes and reduced or waived regulatory fees, more than 500 new drugs for uncommon diseases have reached the market since the law was introduced. For common illnesses, pharmaceutical companies can still generate large profits without charging high prices. For example, Lipitor (atorvastatin), which is used to regulate cholesterol, generates a sales profit of $131 billion while the prescription costs patients around $2 per day. With rare diseases, however, prices must be kept high for the companies to remain in business. As a result, although patients with uncommon illnesses may benefit medically from the new measures, they face high costs. For example, the cystic fibrosis drug Kalydeco by Vertex costs individual patients $311,000.

title: The rebel senator: Can libertarian Rand Paul really conquer a Republican primary?
text: Rand Paul is not like the other would-be presidents. Not even close. The Kentucky senator, who launched his bid for the White House on Tuesday morning, refuses to fit neatly into either party's mold. Socially liberal on crime and punishment, especially drug sentencing, against a federal ban on same-sex marriage, and no foreign policy hawk, he is hardly your typical Republican. Yet as a fiscal conservative and an opponent of abortion rights, he is certainly no Democrat either. "It's time for a new way, a new set of ideas and a new leader," Paul declares in a Web video, set to a heavy metal soundtrack, previewing his presidential campaign. Paul is really a libertarian. And though he is the heir of the last carrier of the torch of "liberty," he is not quite his father's libertarian. His father, former Rep. Ron Paul, ran for president three times before retiring. The elder Paul, 79, was always seen as something of a gadfly, a loud, fresh voice in the Republican primary with a fiercely passionate following of young libertarians. He never won a single state in 2008 or 2012, measured by Election Day vote share, but he routinely finished in the top three. He even took a strong second behind Romney in the critical early state of New Hampshire. And his army of young, engaged and determined Paul-ites proved one thing: they could organize! Ron Paul won straw poll after straw poll at the Conservative Political Action Conference and elsewhere, and he also won the most delegates in several states, including Iowa. Though he finished third in the vote in the Hawkeye State, his campaign pulled off what amounted to a takeover of the state Republican Party machine.

title: Tears and prayers under a blazing sun: two million pilgrims surge to Mount Arafat
text: It was an overwhelming sight. Two million Muslims packed Mount Arafat on Thursday for a vigil to atone for their sins, then streamed down to Muzdalifa to prepare for the final stages of the annual haj pilgrimage. Pilgrims in white robes had spent the night camped at the hill where Islam holds that God tested Abraham's faith by commanding him to sacrifice his son Ismail, and where the Prophet Mohammad gave his last sermon. Other worshippers who had been praying in nearby Mina climbed up by bus or on foot from before dawn, as security forces directed traffic and helicopters hovered overhead. Some of the faithful carved out seats on the rugged hillside, clutching umbrellas against the sun. Others jammed the nearby roads as temperatures soared toward 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit). Men and women from nearly every country on earth stood side by side, some weeping on their neighbor's shoulder. Then came a cry from the hilltop. An elderly Syrian pilgrim shouted out, “Oh God, take revenge on the oppressors.” Those gathered around him answered, “Amen.” Awfa Nejm, from a village near Homs, said: “We ask God to protect Syria and its people and return it to the way it was before.” Twenty-seven-year-old Amin Mohammed from Nigeria said he was praying for peace in his country. The scale is staggering: Saudi Arabia said more than 2.3 million pilgrims, most from outside Saudi Arabia, had arrived for the five-day ritual, a once-in-a-lifetime religious duty for every able-bodied Muslim who can afford the journey. And Sheikh Saad al-Shathri, a senior Saudi cleric, used his midday sermon to denounce terrorism and violence against civilians!

title: Ann Coulter criticizes Delta Air Lines on Twitter after being moved from reserved seat
text: Conservative author and political analyst Ann Coulter, who, like Donald Trump, is described as someone it is unwise to cross, criticized Delta Air Lines on Saturday after the airline removed her from her reserved Comfort+ seat, which provides 3 additional inches of legroom, and gave it to another passenger. In a series of tweets over two hours, she quoted her exchange with a flight attendant. She said she asked: “Why are you taking me out of the extra room seat I specifically booked?” The answer, she said, was “I don't know.” Before Coulter posted a photograph of the woman to whom Delta had given her reserved extra-legroom seat, she wrote on July 16, 2017: “Suckiest [Delta] moved me from my PRE-BOOKED SEAT & gave it to some woman, not elderly, child, or sick. I have pictures so don't lie, [Delta]!” She added: “But at least [Delta] was nice @ it, summarily snatching my ticket from my hand & ordering me to move w/o explanation, compensation or apology” Coulter, who is 6 feet tall and 55 years old, posted a photograph of the woman who received her aisle seat on the flight from LaGuardia to Florida, writing: “Delta didn't give my extra room seat to an air marshal or tall person.”

title: Finally! Pentagon poised to tear down ban on transgender troops
text: One of the military's last walls is about to fall. The Pentagon will announce next month that it is scrapping the policy banning transgender people from serving openly in the military, Defense Department officials said on Friday, ending what is widely seen as one of the last barriers to service. Defense Secretary Ashton B. Carter has blasted the regulation as outdated and harmful to the military. A year ago, he ordered officials from every military branch to work out what changes would be needed to lift the ban, a tacit admission that thousands of transgender people were already in uniform. Under the Pentagon's plan, first reported by USA Today, each branch will put in place policies covering recruiting, housing and uniforms for transgender troops. Officials have been “making great progress, holding multiple meetings and working hard to come up with a policy that balances the needs of soldiers with mission readiness,” said Eric Pahon, a Defense Department spokesman. “They’re trying to come up with something that fits the needs of all of the different services.” And the relief is palpable. Ashley, the president of the American Military Partner Association, a support network for partners and spouses of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender troops and veterans, said in a statement that “our transgender service members and their families are breathing a huge sigh of relief.” How many are affected? Estimates of the number of transgender people in the military range from 2,000 to more than 15,000. Just like the “don’t ask, don’t tell” policy that applied to gay men, lesbians and bisexuals until it was lifted in 2011, the current rules have done little to keep transgender people out of the military. Instead, they have forced many to lie about who they are and keep it secret. Since Carter took over as defense secretary in February 2015, the push has been on.

title: Writer says activists doing all they can should not apologize
text: The author has observed that many allies and accomplices she speaks with about NoDAPL and other struggles describe what they are trying to contribute to the cause and then apologize for not being able to do more. The apologies often appear perfunctory or even insincere, but in some cases they appear heartfelt. The author, who regularly encounters ideological tourists and people who linger at the edges of movements without contributing, states that she is saddened when people who are doing good work feel bad about themselves regardless. They may not be aware of how many people credit themselves for “standing on the right side of history,” as if reading an article or a book and deciding where to “stand,” were the way to affect the course of history. Alternatively, they may not know how to appreciate themselves, or may have been taught not to. The author's message to everyone, whether they regard themselves as an ally, an accomplice or a frontline participant, is that a person who is genuinely doing all that they can has nothing to apologize for. A person who is genuinely doing all that they can is setting a high standard for others. Such a person should recognize that about themselves and accept recognition from others. Although it may sound simple, the author writes, it is often difficult for people to internalize the fact that, in terms of what everyone can contribute, doing all one can is in fact everything.

title: May races to Trump's side: can she revive the legendary 70-year 'special relationship'?
text: A high-stakes meeting! British Prime Minister Theresa May will meet new U.S. President Donald Trump in Washington on Friday, hoping to breathe new life into what London sees as the two countries' “special relationship”. May, the very first foreign leader to visit Trump, wants to forge closer ties with the United States as Britain leaves the European Union. She dreams of the same closeness with him that Margaret Thatcher enjoyed with Ronald Reagan in the 1980s. “Unquestionably, this relationship has assumed way more importance than it might have had even a year ago,” said John Bew, a history and foreign policy professor at King's College London. “Anglo-American relations are back in town in a big way.” But it has never been smooth sailing. The history of the special relationship has always been shaped by personalities, Europe and security issues. The United States declared independence from Britain in 1776, but it was not until 1946 that Winston Churchill coined the term “special relationship” after World War Two. The founding of NATO in 1949 helped deepen military ties, but the alliance hit rough waters in the early years of the Cold War. Then came disaster. In the 1956 Suez Crisis, when Britain attacked Egypt without telling the United States, a furious U.S. President Dwight Eisenhower pressured Prime Minister Anthony Eden to seek a peaceful solution, and Eden ended up resigning. The episode was arguably the worst crisis in U.S.-UK relations of the 20th century, and it showed the British establishment just how far its imperial power had faded and how much it needed to work with the United States in international affairs. The relationship was tested again in 1962, when the administration of U.S. President John Kennedy suddenly canceled its Skybolt missile program, enraging Britain, which had been set to use the missiles.

title: A guide to pokies, the Australian name for slot machines
text: Pokies is the term used in Australia for slot machines. Visitors to Australia who enter a bar, whether in the Outback or in a city, are likely to encounter a pokie machine, and that is when the entertainment begins. Players insert money into the machine, often while heavily intoxicated on Australian beer, and the following day they may wake up not only with a severe headache but with a large amount of cash or, if they are unlucky, with nothing. Players do not need to be in Australia to play pokies, however, as the games can be played online from anywhere. Several types of games are available, including a range of varieties and the traditional classics. Classic: classic slots are popular where they can still be found. They have only one payline, although classic games available today are not necessarily limited to one line. Multiple payline: multiple payline games are widely available, with between 3 and 50 paylines. Activating more paylines by betting more coins gives players more opportunities to form a winning combination and reach the payout. Feature: feature pokies include special symbols that increase a player's chances. Features include wild symbols, scatter symbols, multipliers and jackpot symbols. Collecting a large number of symbols in certain combinations can produce substantial winnings. Bonus: bonus slots are considered a valuable find, because they function as a game within a game.

title: High school vice principal apologizes for Facebook post on domestic terrorism
text: The vice principal of Camden Hills Regional High School wrote in a Facebook post that the country's main threat comes from domestic white Christian men with easy access to guns. After a lone gunman killed two civilians and a police officer in Colorado Springs, Colorado, the vice principal, Piet Lammert, posted the following on Facebook the next day: "It's Small Business Saturday. Buy local. There's a show in the Strom tonight. Buy tickets. The only terrorists we need to fear are domestic white Christian men with easy access to guns. Vote Bernie. That is all. Enjoy your day." The post included an endorsement of Bernie Sanders. Five Town CSD Superintendent Maria Libby criticized the post but defended the administrator. "I know Piet and he's someone who genuinely accepts all people," Libby said. "The post does not reflect who he is as a person." Libby added further comments. "It was a mistake," Libby said. "It was a poor choice in words and it should never have been posted." The superintendent did not specify which words would have been more appropriate. Libby said the situation had been handled after the post was made, but did not provide details. "I have investigated it and I have taken appropriate action," was all Libby would say. Lammert posted on Facebook to apologize to those he had offended and to explain his comments. "I am writing to take responsibility and apologize for a post that I made on my private Facebook account yesterday. I mistakenly left my setting open to Public and in doing so made a post that offended some members of our community and beyond."
